newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Council starts beef aid talks as BSE fears rise.
newsitem.headline: Council starts beef aid talks as BSE fears rise.

text.p: European Union farm ministers began talks on Monday to hammer out measures to help farmers and revive markets staggering from fresh scientific evidence that people can catch mad cow disease.

The evidence, announced by British scientists last week, reinforced the view of EU countries that Britain must respect the Florence European Council agreement on fighting the disease before there could be any easing of a global ban on British beef exports.
"The Florence agreement has to be met. The accelerated cull has to go ahead," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates, whose country holds the EU presidency, told reporters before the meeting.
German, Belgian and Spanish farm ministers agreed.
Under the June agreement, Britain must slaughter up to 147,000 extra cattle to try to eradicate the fatal cattle brain disease, known as Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
But Yates offered a glimmer of hope for Britain.
"If that (cull) goes ahead in one part of the U.K. or Northern Ireland then a regional proposal could be considered," he said, referring to grass-fed herds certified BSE-free.

British Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg, heading a team of five British ministers, will probe EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler's views on a regional easing of the seven-month-old EU ban during private talks at the Council.
"We have identified the beef assurance scheme and certified herds as being those animals for which one could expect first to get a relaxation of the ban," Hogg told reporters.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth stressed the importance for Scottish farmers, noting that one third of agricultural income came from Angus beef and other grass-fed herds.

"We have always made it clear that we will stick to the Florence agreement. We have certainly not ruled out having a cull. We want to make sure that the cull takes account of the latest scientific advice," Forsyth said.
But Fischler cautioned against any early progress.
"I don't think we will achieve very much today because I think we need more time," he told reporters.
Officials said progress was stalled until after EU scientists rule in mid-November on British research casting doubt on whether an extra cull of cattle was needed.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert insisted the British ban must be kept in place.
"There can only be a relaxation if there is no risk coming from British beef exports," Borchert told reporters.
Belgian Farm Minister Karel Pinxten said Belgium had always adopted a very strict stance. "I think it has now been confirmed by the new evidence," he told Reuters.
Spanish Farm Minister Loyola de Palacio said Britain must take all the public health precautions, including the selective cull, agreed in Florence. "Britain must fulfil the terms," she told Reuters.
Fischler stressed the urgent need to agree a package of measures to reduce beef production in line with a drop in demand due to consumer fears that BSE could be passed to people.

But member states remain deeply divided over the proposed measures, which include payments to slaughter new-born calves, and fiercely oppose plans to cover the estimated 1.3 billion Ecus cost by slashing aid to cereals farmers.
Yates said a deal would be difficult and could take days.
"Certainly if we don't reach agreement we shall go very close to it here so that agreement will be in sight," he said.
